claim: Some dragonflies show wax-based color change and ultraviolet (UV) reflection.
source: Some dragonflies show wax-based color change and ultraviolet (UV) reflection, but the biochemical properties underlying the phenomena are totally unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon, supported by existing literature on dragonfly coloration.

claim: The biochemical properties underlying wax-based color change and UV reflection in dragonflies are totally unknown.
source: Some dragonflies show wax-based color change and ultraviolet (UV) reflection, but the biochemical properties underlying the phenomena are totally unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Very long-chain methyl ketones and aldehydes are unique and major wax components in the UV-reflective abdominal wax of dragonflies.
source: Here we investigated the UV-reflective abdominal wax of dragonflies, thereby identifying very long-chain methyl ketones and aldehydes as unique and major wax components.
evidence: This is supported by GC-MS analysis data presented in Figure 5 and related text.

claim: Little wax was detected on young adults of Orthetrum albistylum and O. melania.
source: Little wax was detected on young adults, but dense wax secretion was found mainly on the dorsal abdomen of mature males of Orthetrum albistylum and O. melania
evidence: This is supported by SEM observations and reflectance measurements shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Dense wax secretion was found mainly on the dorsal abdomen of mature males of Orthetrum albistylum and O. melania.
source: Little wax was detected on young adults, but dense wax secretion was found mainly on the dorsal abdomen of mature males of Orthetrum albistylum and O. melania
evidence: This is supported by SEM images in Figure 3 and reflectance data in Figure 2.

claim: Pruinose wax secretion was identified on the ventral abdomen of mature females of O. albistylum and Sympetrum darwinianum.
source: pruinose wax secretion was identified on the ventral abdomen of mature females of O. albistylum and Sympetrum darwinianum.
evidence: This is supported by SEM observations in Figure 3 and chemical analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Comparative transcriptomics demonstrated drastic upregulation of the ELOVL17 gene in wax-producing regions.
source: Comparative transcriptomics demonstrated drastic upregulation of the ELOVL17 gene, a member of the fatty acid elongase gene family, whose expression reflected the distribution of very long-chain methyl ketones.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 10.

claim: ELOVL17 is a member of the fatty acid elongase gene family.
source: Comparative transcriptomics demonstrated drastic upregulation of the ELOVL17 gene, a member of the fatty acid elongase gene family
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 11 and known function of ELOVL proteins.

claim: The expression of ELOVL17 reflected the distribution of very long-chain methyl ketones.
source: Comparative transcriptomics demonstrated drastic upregulation of the ELOVL17 gene, a member of the fatty acid elongase gene family, whose expression reflected the distribution of very long-chain methyl ketones.
evidence: This is supported by comparing transcriptome data in Figure 10 with chemical composition data in Figure 5.

claim: Synthetic 2-pentacosanone spontaneously formed light-scattering scale-like fine structures with strong UV reflection.
source: Synthetic 2-pentacosanone, the major component of dragonfly's wax, spontaneously formed light-scattering scale-like fine structures with strong UV reflection
evidence: This is supported by SEM images and reflectance measurements of synthetic wax in Figure 6.

claim: 2-pentacosanone is the major component of dragonfly's wax.
source: Synthetic 2-pentacosanone, the major component of dragonfly's wax
evidence: This is supported by GC-MS analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Synthetic 2-pentacosanone has potential utility for biomimetics.
source: Synthetic 2-pentacosanone, the major component of dragonfly's wax, spontaneously formed light-scattering scale-like fine structures with strong UV reflection, suggesting its potential utility for biomimetics.
evidence: This is speculative based on the observed properties of synthetic 2-pentacosanone.

claim: Many animals can detect UV light as well as green, blue and/or red light.
source: The diversity of the color patterns encompasses the ultraviolet (UV) range, reflecting the fact that many animals can detect UV light as well as green, blue and/or red light (Osorio and Vorobyev, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Osorio and Vorobyev, 2008.

claim: UV reflection has been reported from numerous organisms.
source: UV reflection has been reported from numerous organisms and may be important not only for protection against UV-induced damage but also for visual signaling (Silberglied, 1979; Eaton and Lanyon, 2003; Paul and Gwynn-Jones, 2003; Lee, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: UV reflection may be important for protection against UV-induced damage and for visual signaling.
source: UV reflection has been reported from numerous organisms and may be important not only for protection against UV-induced damage but also for visual signaling (Silberglied, 1979; Eaton and Lanyon, 2003; Paul and Gwynn-Jones, 2003; Lee, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Previous studies on biological UV reflection have focused on its optical properties and structural bases, such as multilayer surface structures.
source: Previous studies on biological UV reflection have focused on its optical properties and structural bases, such as multilayer surface structures (Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2013.

claim: In some plants and insects, the production and secretion of wax on their surface has been reported to increase UV reflection.
source: In some plants and insects, the production and secretion of wax on their surface has been reported to increase UV reflection (Clark and Lister, 1975; Pope, 1979; Holmes and Keiller, 2002; Kakani et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dragonflies are able to perceive UV light.
source: Because dragonflies are able to perceive UV light (Bybee et al., 2012; Futahashi et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bybee et al., 2012 and Futahashi et al., 2015.

claim: UV color may play important roles in dragonfly mate recognition, male–male competition, habitat selection and behavioral differences.
source: Because dragonflies are able to perceive UV light (Bybee et al., 2012; Futahashi et al., 2015), it seems plausible that UV color also plays important roles in their mate recognition, in male–male competition and in other ecological characteristics such as habitat selection and behavioral differences.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the fact that dragonflies can perceive UV light.

claim: The presence of a pruinose wax layer on the body surface accounts for UV reflection patterns in dragonflies.
source: Several studies have reported that the presence of a pruinose wax layer on the body surface accounts for UV reflection patterns in dragonflies (Silberglied, 1979; Robertson, 1984; Hilton, 1986; Gorb, 1995; Harris et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The biochemical properties and molecular composition of dragonfly wax, and the genes involved in wax production, are totally unknown.
source: but the biochemical properties and molecular composition of the wax, and the genes involved in wax production by dragonflies, are totally unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: In mature females of O. albistylum, moderate UV reflection was observed on the ventral abdomen only.
